sourceEvidence.claim: B cereus entry (full physical order; reheated-rice syndrome; emetic 1-5 h cereulide vs diarrheal 8-18 h; supportive care)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Bacillus cereus

Gram ⊕ rod. Causes food poisoning. Spores survive cooking rice (reheated rice syndrome).
Keeping rice warm results in germination of spores and enterotoxin formation.
Emetic type causes nausea and vomiting within 1-5 hours. Caused by cereulide, a preformed toxin.
Diarrheal type causes watery, nonbloody diarrhea and GI pain within 8-18 hours.
Management: supportive care (antibiotics are ineffective against toxins).
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: C difficile entry part 1 (toxins A/B; pseudomembranous colitis with inline photo marker A; antibiotic and PPI risks; fulminant course)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Clostridioides difficile

Produces toxins A and B, which damage
enterocytes. Both toxins lead to watery diarrhea
→  pseudomembranous colitis A . Often 2°
to antibiotic use, especially clindamycin,
ampicillin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones;
associated with PPIs.
Fulminant infection: toxic megacolon, ileus,
shock.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: C difficile entry part 2 (standalone photo marker A; FA mnemonic; PCR/antigen diagnosis; oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin; fecal microbiota transplant)
sourceEvidence.quote:
A

Difficile causes diarrhea.
Diagnosed by PCR or antigen detection of one
or both toxins in stool.
Treatment: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
For recurrent cases, consider repeating prior
regimen or fecal microbiota transplant.

sourceEvidence.claim: Clostridia genus rule (gram ⊕, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic rods; tetanus and botulinum toxins are SNARE-cleaving proteases)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Clostridia

Gram ⊕, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic rods. Tetanus toxin and botulinum toxin are proteases
that cleave SNARE proteins involved in neurotransmission.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: C tetani entry part 1 (noninvasive, wound-localized; tetanospasmin; retrograde axonal transport; Renshaw-cell GABA/glycine blockade; the spastic triad)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Clostridium tetani

Pathogen is noninvasive and remains localized
to wound site. Produces tetanospasmin, an
exotoxin causing tetanus. Tetanospasmin
spreads by retrograde axonal transport to CNS
and blocks release of GABA and glycine from
Renshaw cells in spinal cord.
Causes spastic paralysis, trismus (lockjaw), risus
sardonicus (raised eyebrows and open grin),
opisthotonos (spasms of spinal extensors).
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: C tetani entry part 2 (FA mnemonic; vaccine prevention; antitoxin +/− booster, antibiotics, diazepam, wound debridement)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Tetanus is tetanic paralysis.
Prevent with tetanus vaccine. Treat with antitoxin
+/− vaccine booster, antibiotics, diazepam (for
muscle spasms), and wound debridement.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: C botulinum entry part 1 (heat-labile SNARE toxin; no ACh at the NMJ; floppy baby vs adult preformed toxin; the 5 D's; no sensory deficits)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Produces a heat-labile toxin that damages
SNARE proteins, thus preventing ACh release
at the neuromuscular junction, causing
botulism. In babies, ingestion of spores (eg, in
honey) leads to disease (floppy baby syndrome).
In adults, disease is caused by ingestion of
preformed toxin (eg, in canned food).
Symptoms of botulism (the 5 D’s): diplopia,
dysarthria, dysphagia, dyspnea, descending
flaccid paralysis. Does not present with
sensory deficits.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: C botulinum entry part 2 (FA mnemonic; human botulinum immunoglobulin; therapeutic Botox uses)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Botulinum is from bad bottles of food, juice,
and honey.
Treatment: human botulinum immunoglobulin.
Local botulinum toxin A (Botox) injections used
to treat focal dystonia, hyperhidrosis, muscle
spasms, and cosmetic reduction of facial
wrinkles.

sourceEvidence.claim: C perfringens entry part 1 (α-toxin lecithinase; myonecrosis/gas gangrene with inline photo marker A and crepitus; the <60°C standing-food rule; 10-12 h enterotoxin)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Produces α-toxin (lecithinase, a phospholipase)
that can cause myonecrosis (gas gangrene A ;
presents as soft tissue crepitus) and hemolysis.
If heavily spore-contaminated food is cooked
but left standing too long at <60°C, spore
germinate →  vegetative bacteria ingested → 
enterotoxin →  late-onset (10-12 hours) food
poisoning symptoms, resolution in 24 hours.

sourceEvidence.claim: C perfringens entry part 2 (FA mnemonic; spontaneous gas gangrene via hematogenous seeding; colonic malignancy; C septicum)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Perfringens perforates a gangrenous leg.
Spontaneous gas gangrene (via hematogenous
seeding; associated with colonic malignancy)
is most commonly caused by Clostridium
septicum.

sourceEvidence.claim: C diphtheriae entry part 1 (angular gram ⊕ rods; respiratory droplets; β-prophage; EF-2 ADP-ribosylation; pseudomembranous pharyngitis with inline photo marker A; bull's neck; myocarditis, arrhythmias, neuropathies; metachromatic granules; ⊕ Elek test; toxoid vaccine)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Gram ⊕ rods occurring in angular
arrangements; transmitted via respiratory
droplets. Causes diphtheria via exotoxin
encoded by β-prophage. Potent exotoxin
inhibits protein synthesis via ADP-ribosylation
of EF-2, leading to possible necrosis in
pharynx, cardiac, and CNS tissue.
Symptoms include pseudomembranous
pharyngitis (grayish-white membrane A ) with
lymphadenopathy (“bull’s neck” appearance).
Toxin dissemination may cause myocarditis,
arrhythmias, neuropathies.
Lab diagnosis based on gram ⊕ rods with
metachromatic (blue and red) granules and
⊕ Elek test for toxin.
Toxoid vaccine prevents diphtheria.

sourceEvidence.claim: L monocytogenes entry (facultative intracellular rod; cold foods and transplacental/vaginal acquisition; cold enrichment; rocket tails with inline photo marker; listeriolysin; tumbling motility; the pregnancy/neonate/immunocompromised disease set; ampicillin)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Gram ⊕, facultative intracellular rod; acquired by ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products and
cold deli meats, transplacental transmission, and by vaginal transmission during birth. Grows well
at refrigeration temperatures (“cold enrichment”).
Forms “rocket tails” (red in A ) via actin polymerization that allow intracellular movement and cellto-cell spread across cell membranes, thereby avoiding antibody. Listeriolysin generates pores in
phagosomes, allowing its escape into cytoplasm. Characteristic tumbling motility in broth.
Can cause amnionitis, sepsis, and spontaneous abortion in pregnant patients; granulomatosis
infantiseptica; meningitis in immunocompromised patients, neonates, and older adults; mild, selflimited gastroenteritis in healthy individuals.
Treatment: ampicillin.
